paras: The lynching of John Taylor took place on the night of June 11-12, 1881, when masked, mounted men broke into the Guilford County jail at Greensboro, North Carolina, and carried off Taylor, a Black farm hand accused of raping a white woman near Reidsville. They hanged him from a roadside oak in Rockingham County, and a coroner's jury found he had been hanged by unknown parties. A Danville wire report noting that the raid came during an eclipse of the moon ran across the country, while North Carolina papers mostly approved the lynching.

According to the Charlotte Democrat, Taylor, 22, and George Gunn, farm hands of Col. James Irwin, went to Irwin's house on June 3 while he was away, and Taylor was accused of assaulting Mrs. Irwin. Both were arrested the next day and, the papers said, confessed before a justice at Reidsville, though Taylor later told a reporter that Gunn was the guilty man. Warned of a lynching party, Sheriff Johnston moved Taylor from the Wentworth jail to Greensboro; the party forced the Wentworth jail and found him gone. An armed party that rode into Greensboro on Monday night also missed him, and the Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic lamented that "the good lessons taught by the Ku Klux in 1871 are forgotten in 1881."

About 11 p.m. on Saturday, June 11, during the eclipse, a body of men entered Greensboro and demanded Taylor at the jail. When jailer O. C. Wheeler refused the keys, they cut through three locked doors with sledges and chisels, overpowered the guard and unchained Taylor from the floor. They tied him to a waiting buggy and rode toward Reidsville as a dozen women waved handkerchiefs from windows.

Seven miles from Reidsville, told that Mrs. Irwin was too ill for a procession to pass her house, the party halted by the road. About 4 a.m. on Sunday, June 12, Taylor was hanged from an oak limb, reportedly from the gray horse he was said to have ridden to the Irwin house. The body hung all day as white and Black visitors came to see it, "not less than 5,000" by the Greensboro Battle Ground's count.

That evening a coroner's jury found that Taylor "had been hanged by unknown parties," and Jupe Billard, a Black man, buried him at the foot of the tree. A Danville dispatch said there was no clue to the lynchers, whom the Battle Ground believed to be Rockingham County men; no report of arrests was found. Gunn, the Farmer and Mechanic wrote, was "allowed the benefit of a regular trial" and remained in jail; no report of the outcome was found. White papers asserted that local Black residents thought the punishment just.

The Danville dispatch ran on June 13 in the Portland Daily Press, the St. Paul Daily Globe, the Chicago Daily Tribune and the Savannah Morning News. These reports stated the rape charge as fact under headlines such as "ECLIPSED" and "A Raylsher [Ravisher] Hanged"; the St. Paul deck spoke of a "Bad Negro" and placed the lynching in Virginia. Weekly digests in Maryland, Alabama and New Jersey repeated short versions into late June.

North Carolina papers wrote at length and mostly endorsed the lynching. Before it happened, the Winston Western Sentinel declared that "the courts should not be bothered" with the accused, and the Farmer and Mechanic headed its account "DEAD AND DONE FOR! DECENTLY AND IN ORDER!", faulting only the delay and the waving handkerchiefs. The Greensboro North State, quoted by the Charlotte Democrat, judged the punishment "well deserved," while the Orange County Observer regretted the occurrence but expected the lynchers would "not be blamed much."

The Danville wire, a Greensboro dispatch and the Battle Ground put the party at about 200, while the Farmer and Mechanic, a News and Observer correspondent and a Reidsville dispatch gave fifty or sixty. The Reidsville dispatch alone dated the raid "Monday night," and one report put the site five miles from Reidsville on the Greensboro road rather than seven. Accounts of the hearing say Taylor confessed, but he later blamed Gunn, and the Farmer and Mechanic wrote that he refused to affirm or deny his guilt.

reader.title: Lynching of John Taylor
bases: A body of masked or disguised men broke into the Greensboro jail, took Taylor from his cell and hanged him from a tree in Rockingham County (A7, A23, A24, A27).

Fifty to two hundred men forced the jail over the jailer's refusal and hanged Taylor, accused of rape, without trial (A7, A24, A27); the coroner's jury found he was 'hanged by unknown parties' and papers framed it as 'Judge Lynch' and 'Speedy Punishment' (A26, A27).

The Danville wire, a separate Greensboro dispatch, the Greensboro Battle Ground, a Reidsville dispatch and a News and Observer correspondent independently agree on the jail break and hanging (A7, A14, A22, A23, A27).

accounts.label: Danville wire
accounts.gist: Taylor, who had 'grossly assaulted' a white woman, was taken during the eclipse by about 200 men who overpowered the guard and hanged him seven miles south of Reidsville; no clue to the lynchers.

accounts.label: Greensboro Battle Ground
accounts.gist: Men met five miles north of town, cut through three locked doors, tied Taylor to a buggy and rode toward Reidsville vowing to hang him there; 'over 200 men'; believed to be Rockingham citizens.

accounts.label: News and Observer correspondent
accounts.gist: Fifty or sixty men hanged Taylor from an oak at 4 a.m.; the body hung all day before crowds; coroner's verdict 'unknown parties'.

accounts.label: Reidsville dispatch
accounts.gist: About sixty masked men took Taylor on 'Monday night'; body found near Troublesome old ironworks seven miles south-west of Reidsville.

accounts.label: Taylor's own statement before the lynching
accounts.gist: Taylor told a reporter that Gunn was the guilty man and that he had stopped short of the house.

framing.detail: The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic headed its account 'DEAD AND DONE FOR! DECENTLY AND IN ORDER!' and had 'no regrets', faulting only the delay.
The Greensboro North State, quoted by the Charlotte Democrat, called Taylor 'a brute' and the punishment 'well deserved'.
The Orange County Observer regretted the occurrence but said the men would 'not be blamed much'.
The Winston Western Sentinel said before the lynching that the courts 'should not be bothered' and headed the later account 'SPEEDY RETRIBUTION'.
Northern and western dailies ran the Danville wire under heads like 'ECLIPSED', 'LYNCHED.' and 'A Raylsher Hanged', stating the assault as fact.

conflicts.note: The smaller figure comes from the accounts that describe the party leaving Greensboro and the hanging itself; the Battle Ground gives 200 as hearsay ('It is said').
Every other account, including local ones, gives Saturday night.
